passage: By Thursday half of Payal's desk at the design office was empty. She had given Nandini her good headphones and the intern her plant. "I won't need them," she said, with a smile that didn't reach her eyes. At lunch in the canteen she pushed her rice around. "Nothing's going to change, Nandu. Not this job, not me. Nothing ever will." Nandini's stomach went cold. She put down her spoon. "Payal, you've been giving your things away. Are you thinking about ending your life?" Payal looked at the table for a long time. Then, very quietly: "Sometimes." Nandini moved her chair closer. "Thank you for telling me. I'm staying with you." Together they walked straight to the staff wellbeing room, where the counsellor saw them at once. Nandini waited outside until the counsellor came out, then sat with Payal while she called her sister, before either of them went home.

qa.q: What did Payal give Nandini?
qa.a: She gave Nandini her good headphones.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when Payal said nothing would ever change?
qa.a: Nandini felt a cold rush of fear and worry, because the giving away and the hopeless words together seemed like serious warning signs.

qa.q: Which of Nandini's steps mattered most?
qa.a: Asking Payal directly and calmly, staying with her, and taking her to the counsellor and her sister that same afternoon instead of waiting to see.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Payal to be asked so directly?
qa.a: It may have been frightening but also a relief to be asked plainly, so she could finally admit what had been on her mind.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone give away belongings and speak hopelessly, asking directly and involving a counsellor and family the same day.

passage: The storm had been blowing for two days when Pista the cat slipped out through the torn window net. Samir, nine, pressed his nose to the glass. "She'll be back tomorrow. Cats always come back." His older sister Mehak bit her lip. The lanes were flooded to the ankle. "Maybe. We could also make posters, just in case." "We don't need posters. She'll come." Next morning Samir ran to the door with the milk saucer. The step was wet and empty. He waited there through breakfast and lunch while the milk went cold. At four he came inside and cried so hard he hiccupped. "You said maybe," he whispered. "I did," Mehak said, sitting down beside him. "Now let's make the posters. Together." He nodded and fetched the crayons.

qa.q: How did Pista get out of the house?
qa.a: She slipped out through the torn window net.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when he found the step empty?
qa.a: He felt crushed and heartbroken after being so sure; he waited all day and then cried until he hiccupped.

qa.q: How did Mehak make room for both hope and reality?
qa.a: She said "maybe" instead of promising, suggested posters just in case, and sat with Samir when his certainty broke.

qa.q: What was it like for Mehak when Samir said posters weren't needed?
qa.a: She was probably worried, knowing the flooded lanes made it uncertain, but she did not want to crush his hope.

grounding: Shows a child certain that his lost cat will return the next day, and the painful moment that rosy certainty meets reality.

passage: Before every exam Gargi announced her doom. "I'm going to fail chemistry. Like, properly fail." On the school bus through Lajpat Nagar she said it again, headphones round her neck. Damini rolled her eyes. "You said that about physics and got seventy-eight." "Exactly. Expect the worst, and then seventy-eight feels like a party." It worked, sort of. Gargi never cried over results. But Damini had noticed something: last night, when the group call went through organic reactions, Gargi logged off at nine. "No point, I'm failing anyway." Today the paper had three organic questions. Gargi came out pale. "That's fine," she said quickly. "I knew I'd fail." But her voice cracked on "knew", and she didn't wait to compare answers.

qa.q: What mark did Gargi get in physics?
qa.a: She got seventy-eight.

qa.q: What did Gargi's cracking voice after the paper suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was more upset and disappointed than she admitted, even though she had told herself to expect the worst.

qa.q: What could Gargi try before the next exam?
qa.a: She could keep her low expectations if they calm her, but still stay for the whole revision call, so low hopes don't turn into low effort.

qa.q: How might Damini see Gargi's doom talk now?
qa.a: Damini found it tiresome at first, but after last night she worries it is quietly costing Gargi real study time.

grounding: Shows a teenager expecting the worst before every exam to protect her feelings, and how that shield quietly cuts her effort.

passage:
"I failed both backlogs again, Urmila. I'll have to repeat the year."
"Arre, don't say it like that! Think positive. Everything happens for good."
"Ammi already told the whole family I'd finish by May."
"See? Negative thinking only. Good vibes, Parveen! Tomorrow is a new day!"
"I just... I'm so tired."
"Tired is a mindset! Come, let's watch something funny on my laptop."
Parveen pulled the blanket up to her chin. "Maybe later."
"Okay, but promise you'll stop being sad, na?"
"Mm."
Urmila went out humming. Parveen picked up her phone, typed "I failed again" to her cousin Hina, looked at it, deleted it, and turned to face the wall.

qa.q: What did Urmila say when Parveen said she was tired?
qa.a: She said, "Tired is a mindset!"

qa.q: How did Parveen feel after Urmila's cheerful replies?
qa.a: She felt more alone and unheard, pulling up the blanket and turning to the wall instead of reaching out.

qa.q: What could Urmila say instead?
qa.a: Something like, "That's really hard. Do you want to tell me what happened?", which lets Parveen share the difficulty instead of hiding it.

qa.q: Why might Urmila keep pushing cheer?
qa.a: She may feel uncomfortable with Parveen's sadness and want to fix it fast, not realising it shuts the conversation down.

grounding: Shows a failing student told to think positive and feeling more alone because the forced cheer brushes past her real difficulty.

passage:
1 June. On the back of a duty roster, Ganga wrote what was actually in the way: night shifts four days a week, four months until the staff nurse exam, and pharmacology, her weakest subject. Jyoti read it over her shoulder. "That's depressing." "No, it's honest. Now the other column." She wrote: swap two nights with Rosamma, forty minutes after every shift, Sunday quizzes with Jyoti.
20 July. The first mock test came back: pharmacology, 41 out of 100. Ganga stared at it, then circled the three chapters where she had lost the most. "Still enough time to fix three chapters."
28 September. Second mock: 68. Not perfect. She added one more Sunday to the plan and went to her shift humming.

qa.q: What did Ganga score in pharmacology in the first mock test?
qa.a: She scored 41 out of 100.

qa.q: How did Ganga feel when the first mock result came back?
qa.a: She was shaken for a moment and stared at it, but stayed steady and confident enough to circle the chapters and plan the fix.

qa.q: What made Ganga's plan stronger than simple positive thinking?
qa.a: She named the real obstacles first, then chose specific steps and adjusted them after each result.

qa.q: How might Jyoti see the list after the second mock?
qa.a: Jyoti might now see that the honest list was useful rather than depressing, since it led to real improvement.

grounding: Shows a young adult naming the real obstacles before an exam, planning what can be done and adapting with confidence.

passage: In the staff room of the government school at Rampura, Ishita suggested turning the empty storeroom into a reading corner. Sarita, who had taught there eleven years, didn't look up from her register. "Be realistic. The children won't come, the books will get stolen, and the headmaster won't sanction anything." Ishita had heard the same line about the kitchen garden in July and the morning radio quiz in August. Each time Sarita sounded wise. Each time nothing was tried. Ishita watched her thumb the edge of the register and remembered hearing that Sarita's own library plan had been scrapped years ago. That evening Ishita cleared one shelf herself and brought six books from home. By Friday, four children were reading there at lunch. Sarita paused in the doorway, then walked on without a word.

qa.q: How long had Sarita taught at the school?
qa.a: She had taught there eleven years.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as Sarita called the idea unrealistic again?
qa.a: Ishita felt frustrated but also curious, noticing that Sarita's "realism" always ended with nothing being tried.

qa.q: What did Ishita's small test show?
qa.a: Clearing one shelf with six books risked very little, and four children reading by Friday gave real evidence instead of predictions.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt pausing in the doorway?
qa.a: She may have felt surprise mixed with an old sting, perhaps remembering her own library plan that was scrapped.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing that a colleague's constant "realism" is really cynicism that never tries anything.

passage: Yogesh, nearly two, had opened every kitchen drawer in the flat. He licked a spoon and tore the pages off an old calendar. On the balcony he stuffed a tulsi leaf into his mouth and made a face. His father, Mridul, had stopped saying "No!" every minute. Instead he had tied the knife drawer shut, moved the cleaning bottles up high, and filled the lowest drawer with lids and spoons, just for Yogesh.

qa.q: Which drawer did Mridul tie shut?
qa.a: He tied the knife drawer shut.

qa.q: What do Yogesh's drawer-opening and leaf-tasting suggest he feels?
qa.a: He seems curious and excited 😊 wanting to find out what everything is, feels like and tastes like.

qa.q: Which of Mridul's choices works better than saying no, and why?
qa.a: Filling a low drawer with lids and spoons, because it gives Yogesh something safe to explore instead of just stopping him.

qa.q: What would change if Mridul kept saying "No!" every minute?
qa.a: Yogesh might get frustrated, Mridul would be worn out, and the dangerous things would still be within reach.

grounding: Shows a toddler exploring by opening, tasting and pulling things apart, and a parent childproofing instead of constantly saying no.

passage:
Monday. In the car, Nitin pressed his face to the window. "Why is the moon following us?" Yogesh Chacha laughed. "Good question! It's so far away that it looks like it moves with us."
Wednesday. "Why is Dadi's skin wrinkly?" "Because she has lived a long time, and skin folds as people get older. You could ask her how old she is."
Saturday. "Why is the sky blue?" Chacha scratched his head. "I don't know exactly. Shall we find out tonight?" That night Nitin fell asleep holding the picture book about sunlight.

qa.q: What did Nitin ask on Wednesday?
qa.a: He asked why Dadi's skin is wrinkly.

qa.q: How was Nitin feeling as he asked all these questions?
qa.a: He was curious and eager 🤔 pressing his face to the window and asking something new each day.

qa.q: Why was "I don't know exactly. Shall we find out?" a good answer?
qa.a: It showed Nitin his question was worth answering and turned not knowing into finding out together.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel if Nitin asks her how old she is?
qa.a: She might feel amused and touched that he is curious about her life.

grounding: Shows a young child's stream of why questions and an adult who treats every one of them as worth answering.

passage:
Tuition notes: Baljeet, Class 4, after six weeks.
In our first sessions Baljeet asked something every few minutes: why fractions get smaller when the bottom number grows, why ants walk in lines. For two weeks now, almost nothing. Today I asked why. Baljeet shrugged, then said, "Suraj Sir said in science to stop asking silly questions and let him finish the chapter. Everyone laughed." Since then Baljeet has been writing questions in the back of a rough notebook instead. There were eleven, including "Do fish sleep?" We spent the last ten minutes on three of them. I told Baljeet those are exactly the kind of questions scientists ask. I will also speak calmly to Suraj Sir at the parents' meeting on Saturday about what I have seen.

qa.q: How many questions were in the back of Baljeet's rough notebook?
qa.a: There were eleven.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling after the class laughed?
qa.a: Baljeet likely felt embarrassed and ashamed of asking, so the questions went into a hidden notebook instead.

qa.q: What did the tutor do that could bring the questions back?
qa.a: Spending time on three of them and calling them scientists' questions showed Baljeet that wondering is welcome.

qa.q: How might Suraj Sir see that moment in science class?
qa.a: Suraj Sir may have seen it as keeping the chapter on track, not realising the remark taught Baljeet to stop asking.

grounding: Shows a child who was told to stop asking silly questions going quiet in class while the curiosity survives privately.

passage: Olga found the books under Oskar's bed in their Gdańsk flat while looking for a lost sock: a Quran in Polish, a book on Buddhism, and a street preacher's pamphlet about the end of the world. Her first feeling was panic. Nobody in their family went to any church. She put the books back and waited until dinner. "I saw your books," she said. "I'm not angry. What got you interested?" Oskar went red, then shrugged. "Everyone at school is so sure about everything. I want to know why." "The end-of-the-world one worries me a bit," Olga admitted. "It worries me too," he said. "That's why I kept it." They talked until the soup went cold. Afterwards he left the Buddhism book on the kitchen table, not under the bed.

qa.q: Where did Olga find the books?
qa.a: She found them under Oskar's bed in their Gdańsk flat.

qa.q: How did Oskar feel when Olga mentioned the books?
qa.a: He was embarrassed at first and went red, but seemed relieved when she wasn't angry and he could explain his curiosity.

qa.q: What made Olga's approach keep the door open?
qa.a: She waited until she was calm, said she wasn't angry, asked what got him interested and admitted her own worry honestly.

qa.q: What would change if Olga had thrown the books away in a panic?
qa.a: Oskar would likely hide his questions and read in secret, with no one to talk to about the pamphlet that worried him.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring religions and a worrying pamphlet out of real interest, and a parent's calm questions keeping talk open.
